prs.title: Remove the experimental.lockDistDir opt-out option
prs.author: bgw
prs.body:
I searched GitHub for people using this opt-out, and it was relatively few: https://github.com/search?q=%22lockDistDir%3A+false%22&type=code

There was one case where it was discovered that the lockfile caused us to error on some network file system implementations (also... why are you building an app on NFS... stop it!). That's fixed in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/100684

Otherwise, everything appeared to be (from looking at comments and commit messages) agents misunderstanding the importance of the lockfile (statements like "we want to run two servers on the same codebase, disable the lockfile").

There's this particularly funny snippet where somebody's agent disabled the feature, and then later wrote a markdown file re-discovering from first principles why this exists and how they now need to be careful to not run multiple serves because it will corrupt itself and crash:

docs/TESTING.md?plain=1#L192-L196

Removing this option removes the footgun. I do not believe that there are any more bugs to be found in the lockfile implementation that require an opt-out to exist.

prs.title: Turbopack: generate require.context as a synthetic module
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

`require.context()` used a hand-written virtual module with its own references and codegen. It is now a synthetic CommonJS source next to the calling module (`<file>.require-context.cjs`) that lists the matched files and `require`s each one. That module goes through normal module handling, so resolution, transforms and chunking all come from the standard paths, and about 270 lines of special-case code go away.

The synthetic source has a source map that maps all of its code to the `require.context()` call, so issues located in it (e.g. a match that fails to resolve) are reported at the call.

Behaviour changes:
- The filter regex is now part of the module ident. Before, two contexts over the same directory with different filters in one file collided.
- Matched files are no longer resolved up front, which also removes a second resolution pass done only for static analysis.
- Like webpack, every file can also be requested without one of the resolve extensions, and a default file (`index`) as its directory, so `keys()` includes `./dir/file` next to `./dir/file.js`. The filter applies to these keys, and they are sorted. This enables the previously disabled "no regex" case of `test/e2e/app-dir/require-context`, which now gives the same keys with both bundlers.

## Performance

This does represent a small performance regression in `require.context` since the synthetic module now goes through the normal module processing path.  The cost isn't parsing (there is more, but

prs.title: Deeply freeze the loaded config in test mode
prs.author: jamiboym
prs.body:
## Summary

When `__NEXT_TEST_MODE` is set, deeply freeze the config returned by `loadConfig` (and the standalone server config) before it is cached. Any later write to the config, or to an object nested in it, then throws where it happens instead of silently changing the config that the rest of the process reads.

The recent config stack removed the known post-load writes (asset prefix, compile mode, export path map, output directories, custom-route metadata). Static checks with deeply readonly config types found no remaining writes, but they cannot see writes through `any`, plain JavaScript, user hooks, or third-party code. Running the test suites with the config frozen covers those for every code path the tests exercise.

The loaded config uses a new `deepFreezePlainValues` export in `shared/lib/deep-freeze.ts`. It matches `deepFreeze` except that it only freezes plain objects and arrays (via the existing `isPlainObject`): class instances such as `RegExp` and `URL` are left alone because freezing breaks them (a global `RegExp` needs a writable `lastIndex`). The standalone config is JSON written at build time, so it uses `deepFreeze` directly.

This only runs in test mode, so it does not change behavior for users. It depends on the previous PR in this stack: without it, freezing the config would also freeze the shared `imageConfigDefault`, and the next `loadConfig` in the same process would throw.

prs.title: Turbopack: narrow async-module emptiness dependencies
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Adds `ModuleGraph::has_async_modules()`, a narrow turbo-tasks accessor that reports whether the module graph contains any async module. The browser and Node.js chunking code now use it when deciding whether to include the async-module runtime helpers, instead of reading the full `AsyncModulesInfo` set just to check whether it is empty.

### Why?

`AsyncModulesInfo` is a keyed cell holding every async module in the graph. Awaiting the whole value makes the reading task depend on every set member, so adding or removing an async module re-ran the runtime/evaluate-chunk tasks even when the result could not change. These callers only care about the empty/nonempty transition.

### How?

The accessor is a memoized task returning a boolean cell. The whole-set read is isolated there; when the set membership changes but stays nonempty, the accessor recomputes the same boolean and downstream chunking tasks are not invalidated. Empty-to-nonempty and nonempty-to-empty changes still invalidate consumers.

The existing runtime inclusion rules are unchanged, including the shared-runtime short-circuits and always including the helpers for the inline browser development runtime. The name follows the existing async-module terminology because the set includes async externals, WASM modules and transitive importers, not only modules with top-level await.

### Verification

- `cargo test -p turbopack-tests --test snapshot` (136 passed, no snapshot changes; includes top-level-await and ru

prs.title: Turbopack: show the source-mapped file in issue headers
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Turbopack issue headers now name the file the reported location belongs to. Both issue formatters, the Turbopack CLI/test-snapshot formatter (`turbopack-cli-utils`) and Next.js `formatIssue`, follow the same rules:

- If the issue has a source, the header shows the source's file, plus a 1-based `line:column` when there is a range.
- If there is no source, the header still shows the issue's own `file_path`.
- The Rust header column is now 1-based, matching Next.js and the additional-sources output. Previously it was 0-based.

Also, since this touches the issue snapshots anyway, the snapshot sanitizer in `turbopack-test-utils` now strips every ANSI escape sequence. Before, it only handled single-number color codes, so multi-parameter codes like the suggestion severity's bold-green-underline stayed in the checked-in snapshots.

### Why?

When an issue is turned into a `PlainIssue`, its source location has already gone through source maps, so the source file can differ from `PlainIssue.file_path`. The formatters used `file_path` for the header but took the line and column from the mapped source. That paired a synthetic Turbopack-internal file name with a position in the original file, and the snippet below it came from a file that was never named. #100535 is an example: the header showed `index.js.import-meta-glob.mjs:5:14`, while the snippet and the issue itself were about the `import.meta.glob` call in `index.js`.

This changes formatting only; no source-map position

prs.title: Turbopack: read block-scoping support during codegen
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

`supports_block_scoping` is now queried during code generation instead of during module analysis.

- `EsmModuleItem::code_generation` reads it from the chunking context's environment, like `supports_arrow_functions` and the ESM/CJS externals checks.
- The eager reads in `analyze_ecmascript_module` and in tracing-mode `cross_module_constants` are removed, along with the `supports_block_scoping` argument/field threaded through `create_graph`, the graph `Analyzer` and `EsmModuleItem`.

### Why?

The value is only used in one place: choosing `const` vs `var` when codegen lowers `export default <expr>`. Reading it before analysis made the analysis task depend on the target environment's runtime versions for no reason, and the tracing-mode read was never used at all (tracing doesn't generate code).

The value now comes from the chunking context's environment rather than the module's compile-time-info environment. For Next.js these are the same: the client, server and edge chunking contexts are built from the matching compile-time-info environments.

### How?

Output is unchanged. Existing snapshots cover both branches: `swc_transforms/preset_env` (`chrome 41`, emits `var`) and `preset_env_modern` and others (emit `const`).

Verification:
- `cargo test -p turbopack-tests --test snapshot`: 136 passed, no snapshot changes. Temporarily forcing `const` made `preset_env` fail, so the codegen-time read is exercised.
- `cargo test -p turbopack-ecmascript`: 618 passed.

prs.title: Turbopack: use flat module context ids for dynamic requests
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

A request with a dynamic part (``require(`./dir/${x}`)``, `require.resolve(...)`, ``import(`./dir/${x}`)``) created its context inline from an object with an `id` and a `module` function per entry, repeating each id twice:

```js
__turbopack_context__.f({ "./dir/a.js": { id: () => "<id>", module: () => __turbopack_context__.r("<id>") }, ... })(key)
```

When every entry is a module (or ignored), it now uses the flat `[key, id, ...]` form that `require.context()` uses (#100526), plus a mode that says how the modules are loaded:

```js
__turbopack_context__.f(["./dir/a.js", "<id>", ...])(key)                   // require
__turbopack_context__.f(["./dir/a.js", "<loader id>", ...], 2).import(key)  // import() via async loaders
__turbopack_context__.f(["./dir/a.js", "<id>", ...], 1).import(key)         // import() without chunk splitting (edge)
```

Every other entry is written as a function that returns its module, using the same per-entry code as before, e.g. one that throws for a request that can't be resolved (`dynamic-unrelated`). Ignored and dropped entries are `undefined`. So the object form is gone from both codegen and runtime, and behavior is unchanged, except that a dropped entry (a target the module graph removed as unused) now requires to `{}` instead of `0`.

`import_externals` is no longer threaded into dynamic imports. It only chose how a raw ESM external is imported, and externals are replaced with wrapper modules (which make that choice themselves) in
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: keep IIFEs with a PURE-annotated callee in production builds
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

In production builds, Turbopack removed side-effecting IIFEs whose callee is a PURE-annotated call, for example `(/* @__PURE__ */ __name(function () { … }, "x"))()`. esbuild emits this shape for `keepNames` output, so Radix UI dists are one affected example.

This PR fixes that, along with the member-expression form `(/* @__PURE__ */ f()).g()`, both with and without scope hoisting.

### Why?

Turbopack runs SWC's `fixer` on every module after codegen, but it passed no comments. SWC's fixer intentionally keeps the parentheses around a PURE / NO_SIDE_EFFECTS-annotated callee or member object, but it can only do that when it can see the comments. Without them it drops the parens.

The printed code then reads `/* @__PURE__ */ f()()`. When the minifier re-parses it, the annotation applies to the outer call, and the whole call is removed as an unused pure expression. webpack is unaffected.

### How?

- **`ReadOnlyComments` adapter** in `swc_comments.rs`. It gives the fixer a read-only view over both the parsed module comments and the comments added by codegen.
  - `has_*` / `get_*` read every store.
  - `has_flag` is overridden to only read. It shares its matcher with `ImmutableComments`, because SWC's default implementation takes the comments and re-adds them.
  - `add_*`, `take_*` and `add_pure_comment` panic, so the adapter can't be used where comments really need to change.
  - `move_*` are deliberate no-ops: the fixer calls them for every pair of parentheses it remo
…(truncated)

prs.title: [ci] Resolve the PR to comment on from the workflow run alone
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
`PR CI Comment` trusted the artifact from an untrusted producer: the workflow on a PR.

While the PR comment is informative only, it was still subject to vandalism and phishing.

The artifact is gone, along with the `pr-ci-metadata` job that produced it and the download step. The target is resolved from `head_repository` and `head_branch`, which GitHub mints into the `workflow_run` payload: `GET /pulls?head={owner}:{branch}`, preferring open pull requests and falling back to any state only for a pull request whose head is the exact commit the run reported on.

The obvious alternatives were checked against the live API first, because they do not work:

| source | fork PRs |
| --- | --- |
| `commits/{sha}/pulls` | returns `[]` |
| `workflow_run.pull_requests` | empty, and sometimes empty for branch PRs too |
| `pulls?head={owner}:{branch}` | resolves |

That is why the artifact existed in the first place.

### Behavior changes

- Runs that ran no jobs (`cancelled`, `action_required`, `startup_failure`) are skipped. They previously resolved no pull request and silently did nothing. Now that fork runs resolve, they would otherwise post an empty `## Failing CI jobs` report. This also fixes that happening today on branch PRs, where a force push leaves a `cancelled` run that rewrites the comment that way.
- A run that comes back completed after a new commit reached the pull request head stays silent, now as an explicit staleness check rather than a side effect of validating identity

prs.title: experimental_prepare: Don't refetch on commit due to stale inlining hints
prs.author: acdlite
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes a narrow case where committing a prepared navigation (`router.experimental_prepare()`) fetches the route a second time.

It only happens when the route wasn't already in the route cache when the prepare started, and the page was prerendered at build time. Build-time prerenders are marked with `InliningHintsStale`, which causes the client to write their route cache entry already expired. So when the commit looks up the route, it misses the entry the prepare just wrote, and fetches the route again.

To fix this, the prepare saves the result of its route request on the preparation record, and the commit uses it instead of making a new request. It's subject to the same checks as taking over an in-flight request.

This is a workaround for `InliningHintsStale`. Once that mechanism is removed, this can be too.

Alternative to #101163; test cases adapted from that PR.

## Verification

- Not run: `pnpm test-start-turbo test/e2e/app-dir/prepare-navigation/prepare-navigation.test.ts` (left to CI)

prs.title: Turbopack: retry chunk loads that failed with component chunks
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

With `experimental.turbopackChunking.generateComponentChunks` enabled, a dynamic `import()` whose chunk fails to load (for example because the network drops) never loads again until a full page reload. Calling the same `import()` again after the network is back rejects immediately with the same `ChunkLoadError`, and no new chunk request is made. With the flag off, the retry refetches the chunk and resolves.

**Cause:** with component chunks enabled, async-loader chunk data carries `moduleChunks`, so loading goes through `loadComponentChunksOrWhole` in the browser runtime (`runtime-base.ts`). That function caches the load promise in `availableModuleChunks` for each component chunk. A rejected promise was never evicted, so on retry every component looked "available" and the split path just re-awaited the cached rejections. Without component chunks, the chunk data is a plain path that goes straight to the DOM backend, and the backend already drops failed loads.

**Fix:** the runtime's base-layer load caches (`availableModules`, `availableModuleChunks`, `splitChunkPromises`) now add entries through a small `cacheLoadPromise` helper. It stores the original promise, so in-flight/successful dedup and the promise identity React relies on are unchanged. It removes the entry when the promise rejects, but only if the entry still holds that same promise. The `ChunkLoadError` itself and the backend's existing single automatic retry are unchanged.

**Places updated:**

- `turbo
…(truncated)

prs.title: Automatically compress route handler responses if not already compressed
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
Route handler responses were never compressed when self-hosted.

`NodeNextResponse.appendHeader` stored every header value as an array, even a single value. The compression middleware checks `Content-Type` with the `compressible` package, which only accepts strings, so any response sent through `sendResponse` (all app route handlers, including prerendered ones served from the cache) failed the content-type filter and skipped compression. `appendHeader` now keeps a single value as a plain string, matching Node's own `appendHeader` semantics.

Fixes https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/101120
Closes https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101201
We must strip CE and CL headers from `Response` returned from route handlers due to https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-pc58-hwjq-p385. A `Response` from `fech()` is indistinguishable from a synthetic one. Any provenance can get lost via `clone` or manual reconstruction based on headers and body.
Instead, the responses from route handlers should be returned uncompressed and be compressed by the outgoing server: now `next start` or your hosting provider e.g. Vercel.

Route handlers should not return a `fetch()` without processing the body as this needlessly adds CPU overhead due to `fetch()`'s automatic decompression. Use a dedicated proxy library for that instead.

## test plan

- moved dev-only compression test to e2e and extended with small/large and dynamic/static routes

prs.title: [turbopack] Fix GC/eviction race by dropping task resurrection
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Fix a panic in development: `connect_child` → `increase_active_count` hit a task that GC had collected and eviction had already removed (`task is missing in memory or persistent storage`).

**The race.** GC marks tasks deleted under the snapshot exclusion. The exclusion is released before the snapshot commits the tombstones, and eviction then removes the deleted tasks with no exclusion. A concurrent `get_or_create_task` could read a deleted task's id from the in memory `task_cache`, eviction could remove the task, and the connect would then panic. Resurrection only worked if the connect finished before eviction.

**The fix.** A deleted task's id is never handed out again from the disk cache:
- GC removes collected tasks from `task_cache` while operations are still excluded.
- `task_by_type` skips candidates that are deleted or already gone.
    - This is only possible for calls that race with snapshotting.  We treat deleted tasks as absent (in other words like the commit already happened).
- Eviction no longer touches `task_cache` for deleted tasks. (it doesn't need to, there are no entries)

**Resurrection is removed.**  The only thing resurrection is really saving is allocating a new `TaskId` (cells and edges are already gone), so it is simpler to remove this path.

Since nothing outside GC can legitimately reach a deleted task now, `ExecuteContext::task` and `task_or_create` debug-assert against one, except when we are running GC, since GC marks tasks deleted a
…(truncated)

prs.title: Add a server-router regression gate: pnpm test-routing
prs.author: jamiboym
prs.body:
## Summary

`pnpm test-routing` runs the e2e tests that check the server's routing and HTTP behavior, first with `next start` and then with `next dev`, through the existing `run-tests.js`. The suite passes on today's server, so a failure after a change to the server is a regression. It's the gate for consolidating the server and routing implementation.

- `test/routing-tests-manifest.json` is a v2 test manifest of whole files: every test under `test/e2e/routing-server/`, plus 69 existing suites that mostly test server routing. That's 87 files; start mode runs 86 and dev runs 80. Nothing is selected by test name, and a manifest entry that matches no file fails the run.
- `scripts/test-routing.mjs` expands the manifest into explicit paths for each mode and sets the same bundler environment as the CI jobs. Turbopack is the default; `--bundler=webpack` and `--bundler=rspack` also work, and the Rspack manifests narrow the list. It turns `run-tests.js` retries off when a selected test directory has unstaged changes, because a retry resets that directory with `git clean -fdx`.

prs.title: [image-optimizer] Don't use NextConfigComplete for the imageOptimizerTransform public API
prs.author: bgw
prs.body:
